name: Kings Canyon National Park
blurb: Giant sequoias, mule deer and the mountain lions of the high Sierra.

tip.title: Take away fire
tip.text: Sequoias need fire to open cones and clear rivals. Set Fire to -100% and watch sequoia, fireweed and the animals that rely on them.

sources.title: NPS: Mammals of Sequoia and Kings Canyon

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Short, snowy winters and bright summers set the growing season for plants from the foothills to the high country.
Heavy winter snow melts in May and June and feeds the streams and meadows. Streams usually shrink to a trickle by autumn.
Sequoias need periodic fire to open cones and clear competing growth. A century of fire suppression let fuel build up.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down fallen needles, wood, carcasses and droppings and return nutrients to the forest soil.
A tall wildflower that spreads quickly across burned ground. Its nectar draws bees and deer browse it.

nodes.name: Meadow sedges & grasses
nodes.desc: Grass-like plants of Sierra meadows and high slopes that feed marmots, voles and bighorn sheep.
Browses shrubs, wildflowers and oak. Wikipedia says that when predators declined in the early 1900s, deer numbers spiked and overgrazed the understory.
A large ground squirrel of meadows and talus that eats grasses and wildflowers and hibernates through winter.
Eats seeds, fungi, fruit and insects, and is prey for hawks and bears.
Wikipedia says it gnaws young sequoia cones year-round, dropping some seeds as it feeds.
A small rodent of damp meadows that eats grasses and other green plants and is prey for hawks.
An abundant small rodent that eats seeds and insects and is prey for hawks and snakes.
Several bumble bee species feed on flower nectar and pollen, and visit wildflowers such as fireweed.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats berries, nuts, insects, carrion and young deer. In the park it often seeks human food near campgrounds.
A clever omnivore and scavenger and the most recorded bird in the area. It picks over carcasses.
Hunts squirrels, marmots, mice and voles from the air, and has the widest list of prey recorded in GloBI here.

nodes.name: Northern Pacific rattlesnake
nodes.desc: Ambushes mice, small marmots and lizards on warm, rocky slopes.

nodes.name: Mountain lion
nodes.desc: The park's main large predator. It hunts mule deer and is a major threat to Sierra Nevada bighorn sheep.
